newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Canberra tips exodus from telecom giants.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canberra tips exodus from telecom giants.

text.p: The Australian government predicted on Wednesday an exodus of customers from the big telecoms carriers to their smaller competitors when the market was deregulated from July 1.
Communications Minister Richard Alston said many customers were already leaving telecoms carriers Telstra Corp and Optus Communications Pty Ltd for newer, cheaper telephone companies.

"The exodus can be expected to accelerate after July when business phone companies such as AAPT, plus electricity suppliers and other utilities start to offer low-cost services to consumers and new players enter the market," he told reporters.
AAP Telecommunications Pty Ltd is the third largest carrier in Australia.
Alston said increasing competition was already delivering lower prices, more choices and better services to Australians.
"But it is just a taste of what is to come," he said.
Australia took the first step towards telecoms deregulation in the early 1990s when it allowed a single competitor to set up against Telstra, the government-owned monopolist.
The then Labor government then allowed Vodafone a third mobile telephone network and targeted July 1, 1997, as the beginning of completely open competition within the industry.

Alston's Liberal-National administration last year set out the regulatory system for the new competitive regime, under which there would be no limit on the number of carrier licences issued and no restrictions on the services they could provide.
But Alston said these benefits still depended on the succesful passage of the deregulation legislation through the upper house of parliament, the Senate, which the government does not control.
Debate on the legislation was scheduled for next Monday and Alston said he was hopeful of making good progress.
He also said the government was considering some amendments to the legislation suggested by the Labor Opposition and the minor Democrats party.
"While I cannot give you any details as yet, I think you will see that we will take some of these suggestions on board," he said.

Optus Communications is 25 percent owned by Mayne Nickless Ltd, while Britain's Cable & Wireless Plc and United States telephone carrier BellSouth Corp Inc both own 24.5 percent. The rest is held by Australian institutions.
